levels.intro: A1 is the present tense and the agreement system. There is no past tense at this level and no imperative: everything you can say, you say now. What you gain instead is the machinery that never goes away, gender and number running through the article and the adjective, the four irregular verb families, the ser and estar split, and the written accent.

topics.title: Sounds and spelling
topics.summary: Five vowels with one sound each and no reduction. ñ, ll and rr are distinct letters or digraphs that change meaning. h is always silent, v and b are the same sound. In the Castilian model taught here, c before e or i and z are pronounced as the th of think, distinct from s; seseo merges them and is standard in Andalusia, the Canaries and all of America.
tables:
ca que qui co cu      za ce ci zo zu
ga gue gui go gu      ja ge gi jo ju
                      güe güi (diaeresis makes the u sound)

examples.target: El perro pequeño corre.
examples.gloss: The little dog runs.

examples.target: Hoy hace calor en la ciudad.
examples.gloss: It is hot in the city today.

topics.title: Stress and the written accent
topics.summary: Words ending in a vowel, n or s are stressed on the second-to-last syllable; all others on the last. A word that breaks that rule carries a written accent, and any word stressed three syllables from the end always carries one. A second use of the accent separates one-syllable words that are otherwise identical.
tables:
ends in vowel/n/s -> stress 2nd-last   casa, hablan, lunes
ends in other consonant -> stress last  hablar, ciudad, reloj
breaks the rule -> write the accent     habló, árbol, lápiz
3rd from the end -> always written      teléfono, música

examples.target: Hablo español, pero él habló inglés.
examples.gloss: I speak Spanish, but he spoke English.

topics.title: Gender of nouns
topics.summary: Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine and those in -a usually feminine. Endings in -ción, -sión, -dad and -tad are always feminine. Nouns in -e or a consonant may be either and must be learned with their article. A frequent group breaks the pattern: el día, el problema, el mapa, el idioma, la mano.
tables:
el libro     la casa
el peine     la muerte
el árbol     la catedral
el día       la mano      (exceptions)

examples.target: La ciudad es grande y el problema es pequeño.
examples.gloss: The city is big and the problem is small.

topics.title: Number of nouns
topics.summary: Add -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant. A final -z becomes -ces. Words already ending in unstressed -s do not change in the plural.
tables:
libro  -> libros     ciudad -> ciudades
casa   -> casas      lápiz  -> lápices
lunes  -> lunes      café   -> cafés

examples.target: Los lápices están en la mesa.
examples.gloss: The pencils are on the table.

topics.title: Definite and indefinite articles
topics.summary: el, la, los, las and un, una, unos, unas, all agreeing with the noun. Feminine nouns beginning with a stressed a take el in the singular for pronunciation: el agua, but las aguas and el agua fría. Spanish also uses no article at all where English uses one, notably with professions after ser.
tables:
masc sg  fem sg   masc pl  fem pl
definite    el       la       los      las
indefinite  un       una      unos     unas
contractions: a + el = al      de + el = del

examples.target: Soy profesora y trabajo en el centro de la ciudad.
examples.gloss: I am a teacher and I work in the city centre.

topics.title: Adjectives: agreement and position
topics.summary: Adjectives agree with their noun in gender and number. Those ending in -o have four forms; those in -e or a consonant vary only for number. The default position is after the noun. Placing the adjective first turns a fact into a judgement, and a few adjectives shorten before a masculine singular noun.
tables:
alto  alta  altos  altas
grande  grande  grandes  grandes
azul  azul  azules  azules
bueno -> buen hombre    grande -> gran hombre

examples.target: Es un hombre grande, pero no es un gran hombre.
examples.gloss: He is a big man, but he is not a great man.

topics.title: Subject pronouns and forms of address
topics.summary: yo, tú, él, ella, usted, nosotros, nosotras, vosotros, vosotras, ellos, ellas, ustedes. Spain uses four second persons: tú and vosotros informally, usted and ustedes formally. Latin America has no vosotros and uses ustedes for every plural. Subject pronouns are normally omitted because the verb ending already carries the person, and are used only for contrast or to remove ambiguity.
tables:
informal      formal
singular tú            usted
plural   vosotros/as   ustedes   (Spain)
plural   ustedes       ustedes   (Latin America)

examples.target: Yo trabajo por la mañana y tú trabajas por la tarde.
examples.gloss: I work in the morning and you work in the afternoon.

topics.title: The present indicative: regular verbs
topics.summary: Three conjugations with one ending set each. The stress falls on the ending in nosotros and vosotros and on the stem everywhere else, which is the fact that explains the irregular families.
tables:
hablar             comer            vivir
hablo   hablamos   como   comemos   vivo   vivimos
hablas  habláis    comes  coméis    vives  vivís
habla   hablan     come   comen     vive   viven

examples.target: Vivimos en Madrid y trabajamos cerca de casa.
examples.gloss: We live in Madrid and we work near home.

topics.title: The present indicative: the four irregular families
topics.summary: Three families change the stem vowel wherever the stress lands on the stem, so the change appears in every form except nosotros and vosotros. The fourth family is irregular in the yo form only. Learning the families rather than the verbs means a new verb declares itself the first time you see it conjugated.
tables:
e > ie   quiero quieres quiere queremos queréis quieren
o > ue   puedo puedes puede podemos podéis pueden
e > i    pido pides pide pedimos pedís piden
yo only  hago pongo salgo traigo conozco sé veo doy

examples.target: No puedo ir porque tengo que trabajar.
examples.gloss: I cannot go because I have to work.

topics.title: ser, estar and hay
topics.summary: ser states what something is: identity, origin, profession, material, the time and the date. estar states what state it is in: location, mood, condition and the result of an action. hay is an invariable form meaning there is or there are, used for existence with indefinite or unquantified nouns and never with a definite article.
tables:
ser    soy eres es somos sois son
estar  estoy estás está estamos estáis están
hay    (invariable, all persons and numbers)

new information -> hay + un/una/dos/mucho
known information -> está + el/la

examples.target: Es de Sevilla, pero ahora está en Bilbao.
examples.gloss: He is from Seville, but he is in Bilbao now.

examples.target: ¿Hay un banco por aquí? ¿Dónde está el banco?
examples.gloss: Is there a bank around here? Where is the bank?

topics.title: Question words and question form
topics.summary: qué, quién, quiénes, dónde, cómo, cuándo, cuánto, por qué. All carry a written accent when they ask. A question opens with ¿ and closes with ?, and no auxiliary verb is added: the word order and the intonation do the work. por qué asks and porque answers.
tables:
¿Qué?      ¿Quién?    ¿Dónde?
¿Cómo?     ¿Cuándo?   ¿Cuánto/a/os/as?
¿Por qué?  ->  Porque...

examples.target: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque mi trabajo está en España.
examples.gloss: Why are you studying Spanish? Because my job is in Spain.

topics.title: Negation
topics.summary: no goes immediately before the verb. Spanish requires a double negative: when nada, nadie, nunca, ninguno or tampoco follow the verb, no must still appear in front of it. If the negative word comes first, no is dropped.
tables:
No viene nadie.      =  Nadie viene.
No hay nada.         =  Nada hay. (rare, literary)
No voy nunca.        =  Nunca voy.

examples.target: No conozco a nadie aquí y no hablo nunca con los vecinos.
examples.gloss: I do not know anyone here and I never talk to the neighbours.

topics.title: Possessives and demonstratives
topics.summary: Unstressed possessives agree with the thing possessed, not with the owner: mi, tu, su, nuestro, vuestro, su. su is ambiguous between his, her, your formal and their, and is disambiguated with de él, de ella, de usted. Demonstratives mark three distances: este here, ese there by you, aquel over there.
tables:
mi(s)  tu(s)  su(s)  nuestro/a(s)  vuestro/a(s)  su(s)

este  esta  estos  estas    (near me)
ese   esa   esos   esas     (near you)
aquel aquella aquellos aquellas  (far from both)

examples.target: Este es mi coche y aquella es la casa de mis padres.
examples.gloss: This is my car and that over there is my parents' house.

topics.title: gustar and the verbs that work backwards
topics.summary: gustar does not mean to like, it means to be pleasing, so the thing liked is the grammatical subject and the person is an indirect object. The verb therefore agrees with the thing, giving only two common forms, gusta and gustan. The pronoun me, te, le, nos, os, les is obligatory, and a mí, a ti, a Ana may be added for emphasis or clarity.
tables:
(A mí)      me   gusta el café / gustan los libros
(A ti)      te
(A él/ella) le
(A nosotros) nos
(A vosotros) os
(A ellos)   les

examples.target: A mí me gusta el cine, pero a mi hermano le gustan los deportes.
examples.gloss: I like the cinema, but my brother likes sports.

topics.title: The first verb chains
topics.summary: Four high-frequency structures take an infinitive directly and give the learner a future, an obligation and a modality long before those tenses exist: ir a for what is going to happen, tener que for personal obligation, hay que for impersonal obligation, and querer or poder for wanting and being able.
tables:
voy a + infinitive        what is going to happen
tengo que + infinitive    I have to
hay que + infinitive      one has to (impersonal)
quiero / puedo + infin.   I want to / I can

examples.target: Mañana voy a hablar con el jefe porque tengo que pedir unos días.
examples.gloss: Tomorrow I am going to speak to the boss because I have to ask for some days off.

levels.intro: A2 is where Spanish acquires a past and a voice of command. Three past tenses arrive and have to be told apart, the object pronouns arrive and have to be ordered, and the imperative arrives and turns out to depend on both. This is the level Spain's nationality procedure asks for, and it is the level where most of the everyday language actually lives.

topics.title: Reflexive verbs
topics.summary: The pronoun matches the subject and normally sits before the conjugated verb. Beyond genuine reflexives (lavarse, ducharse) the same machinery covers daily-routine verbs, changes of state (ponerse, quedarse), reciprocal actions (se conocen) and verbs whose meaning shifts with the pronoun (ir against irse).
tables:
levantarse
me levanto   nos levantamos
te levantas  os levantáis
se levanta   se levantan

voy a levantarme  =  me voy a levantar

examples.target: Me levanto a las siete y me ducho antes de desayunar.
examples.gloss: I get up at seven and I shower before having breakfast.

topics.title: estar plus gerundio
topics.summary: For an action in progress at the moment of speaking. The gerund is -ando for -ar verbs and -iendo for -er and -ir, with the irregulars leyendo, oyendo, durmiendo, pidiendo, diciendo. Spanish uses it far less than English does: the plain present already covers habit and general truth, so estoy trabajando means right at this moment and not this year.
tables:
hablar -> hablando     leer   -> leyendo
comer  -> comiendo     dormir -> durmiendo
vivir  -> viviendo     pedir  -> pidiendo

examples.target: No puede ponerse, está hablando por teléfono.
examples.gloss: He cannot come to the phone, he is on a call.

topics.title: Direct and indirect object pronouns
topics.summary: The two sets differ only in the third person. Placement: before a conjugated verb, or attached to an infinitive, gerund or affirmative imperative, with both positions valid in a two-verb structure. When both appear the indirect comes first, and le or les becomes se before lo, la, los, las. Spanish also doubles the indirect object with its noun, which English never does.
tables:
direct    me te lo/la nos os los/las
indirect  me te le    nos os les

le + lo  ->  se lo      NEVER le lo
Lo veo. / Quiero verlo. / Estoy viéndolo. / Míralo.
Lo tengo que hacer.  =  Tengo que hacerlo.

examples.target: Le doy el libro a Ana. Se lo doy mañana.
examples.gloss: I am giving the book to Ana. I will give it to her tomorrow.

topics.title: The pretérito perfecto
topics.summary: haber in the present plus an invariable participle. It places an event inside a stretch of time that reaches the present: hoy, esta semana, este año, ya, todavía no, alguna vez, nunca. This is the peninsular pattern; most of Latin America uses the indefinido in these same contexts, which is a variety difference and not an error.
tables:
he hablado    hemos hablado
has hablado   habéis hablado
ha hablado    han hablado

irregular participles:
hecho escrito visto puesto dicho vuelto abierto roto

examples.target: Esta semana he trabajado mucho, pero todavía no he terminado.
examples.gloss: This week I have worked a lot, but I have not finished yet.

topics.title: The pretérito indefinido
topics.summary: For an event inside a period that is closed: ayer, anoche, el año pasado, en 2019, hace dos años. The regular forms depend entirely on their written accents. A group of very frequent verbs has an irregular stem and a set of unstressed endings that carry no accent at all, and ser and ir share one form.
tables:
hablar             comer/vivir
hablé   hablamos   comí     comimos
hablaste hablasteis comiste  comisteis
habló   hablaron   comió    comieron

strong stems: tuv- estuv- hic- pud- pus- vin- quis- sup- dij- traj-
endings: -e -iste -o -imos -isteis -ieron  (dij- and traj- take -eron)
ser / ir: fui fuiste fue fuimos fuisteis fueron

examples.target: Ayer fuimos al museo y luego cenamos en el centro.
examples.gloss: Yesterday we went to the museum and then had dinner in the centre.

topics.title: The pretérito imperfecto
topics.summary: For description, background, habit, age, weather and the time of day, with no endpoint in view. Only three verbs in the language are irregular here. In narrative it sets the scene while the indefinido moves the action.
tables:
hablaba  hablábamos     comía   comíamos
hablabas hablabais      comías  comíais
hablaba  hablaban       comía   comían

ser: era eras era éramos erais eran
ir:  iba ibas iba íbamos ibais iban
ver: veía veías veía veíamos veíais veían

examples.target: Llovía cuando salí de casa.
examples.gloss: It was raining when I left the house.

topics.title: Choosing between the three past tenses
topics.summary: The decision is made in two steps. First, is the time period closed or does it reach now? Closed takes the indefinido, open takes the perfecto. Second, are you reporting an event or describing a state? Reporting takes the indefinido, describing takes the imperfecto. Time markers are the most reliable signal, and a single story normally uses all three.
tables:
hoy, esta semana, ya, nunca, alguna vez  -> he hablado
ayer, anoche, en 2019, hace un año       -> hablé
description, habit, age, weather, time   -> hablaba

examples.target: Ayer conocí a su hermana. Era muy simpática y hablaba tres idiomas.
examples.gloss: Yesterday I met his sister. She was very nice and spoke three languages.

topics.title: The affirmative imperative
topics.summary: The tú form is the third person of the present, with eight irregulars. The vosotros form is the infinitive with its final r replaced by d, and it exists only in Spain. The usted and ustedes forms come from the present subjunctive. Pronouns attach to the end and often force a written accent so the stress does not shift.
tables:
hablar   comer    escribir
tú       habla    come     escribe
vosotros hablad   comed    escribid
usted    hable    coma     escriba
ustedes  hablen   coman    escriban

irregular tú: di haz pon sal ten ven sé ve
compra + lo -> cómpralo     da + me + lo -> dámelo

examples.target: Sigue todo recto y gira a la derecha en la segunda calle.
examples.gloss: Go straight on and turn right at the second street.

topics.title: Comparatives and superlatives
topics.summary: más que, menos que and tan como for adjectives and adverbs; tanto, tanta, tantos, tantas como for nouns. Four adjectives have irregular comparatives. The relative superlative is el más de, and the absolute superlative adds -ísimo without comparing anything.
tables:
más alto que    menos caro que    tan alto como
tanto dinero como    tantas casas como

bueno -> mejor    malo -> peor
grande -> mayor   pequeño -> menor

el más alto de la clase      altísimo

examples.target: Este piso es más caro que el otro, pero no es tan grande.
examples.gloss: This flat is more expensive than the other one, but it is not as big.

topics.title: Adverbs, and muy against mucho
topics.summary: Adverbs of manner are formed by adding -mente to the feminine form of the adjective, and when two appear in a row only the second keeps the suffix. muy modifies adjectives and adverbs and never stands alone; mucho modifies verbs and, with agreement, nouns.
tables:
rápido -> rápida -> rápidamente
lento y claro -> lenta y claramente

muy + adjective/adverb:  muy cansado, muy bien
mucho + verb:            trabajo mucho
mucho/a/os/as + noun:    mucha gente, muchos libros

examples.target: Habla muy rápido, así que trabajo mucho para entenderlo.
examples.gloss: He speaks very fast, so I work hard to understand him.

topics.title: Stressed possessives and relative que
topics.summary: The stressed possessives mío, tuyo, suyo, nuestro, vuestro follow the noun or stand alone after ser, and agree with the thing possessed. Relative que joins two clauses and covers both people and things; the fuller relative system arrives at B1.
tables:
un amigo mío      Este libro es mío.
la culpa es tuya  Los nuestros llegan tarde.

El libro que compré ayer.
La chica que vive arriba.

examples.target: Un amigo mío tiene un piso que está muy cerca del centro.
examples.gloss: A friend of mine has a flat that is very near the centre.

topics.title: Indefinites and quantifiers
topics.summary: algo and nada, alguien and nadie, alguno and ninguno, plus todo, otro, cada, demasiado, bastante and poco. alguno and ninguno shorten to algún and ningún before a masculine singular noun, and ninguno is almost always singular even where English uses a plural.
tables:
algo / nada          alguien / nadie
algún libro / ningún libro
alguna casa / ninguna casa
todo el día / todos los días
otro coche (never *un otro coche)

examples.target: No hay ningún problema, pero necesito otra semana.
examples.gloss: There is no problem at all, but I need another week.

topics.title: Time clauses and expressions of duration
topics.summary: cuando plus the present for a habit; antes de and después de plus an infinitive when both clauses share a subject; desde for a starting point, desde hace for elapsed time, and hace que for how long something has been going on. The future use of cuando needs the subjunctive and belongs to B1.
tables:
Cuando viene, trae regalos.        (habit)
antes de salir / después de cenar  (same subject)
desde 2019    desde hace dos años
Hace dos años que vivo aquí.
Vivo aquí desde hace dos años.

examples.target: Trabajo aquí desde hace tres años, y antes de venir vivía en Valencia.
examples.gloss: I have been working here for three years, and before coming I lived in Valencia.

topics.title: Cause and purpose
topics.summary: porque answers why and never begins a sentence in that use; como states a cause and always comes first; es que softens an excuse in speech. Purpose with a shared subject takes para plus an infinitive. por and para begin to divide here: cause and exchange against destination and purpose.
tables:
Estudio español porque trabajo en Madrid.
Como llueve, no salimos.
No voy, es que estoy cansado.
Estudio para aprobar el examen.

por: cause, exchange, route, duration, means
para: destination, purpose, deadline, recipient

examples.target: Trabajo para ella, pero hoy estoy aquí por ella.
examples.gloss: I work for her, but today I am here on her behalf.

topics.title: The verb pairs English collapses
topics.summary: saber is knowing a fact or having a skill, conocer is being acquainted with a person, place or work. pedir asks for a thing, preguntar asks a question. Both pairs are single verbs in English and mixing them is the most visible A2 error.
tables:
saber + fact / + infinitive:  sé la respuesta, sé nadar
conocer + person/place:       conozco a Ana, conozco Madrid

pedir + thing:      pedir un café, pedir ayuda
preguntar + question: preguntar la hora, preguntar por alguien

examples.target: Conozco a su hermano, pero no sé dónde vive.
examples.gloss: I know his brother, but I do not know where he lives.

topics.title: The gustar class in full
topics.summary: encantar, interesar, molestar, doler, parecer, apetecer and faltar all take the same shape as gustar: an indirect object pronoun and a verb agreeing with the thing. doler is the one that matters most in practice, because it is how Spanish talks about pain.
tables:
me encanta / me encantan
me interesa / me interesan
me duele la cabeza / me duelen los pies
me parece bien / me parecen caros
me apetece un café

examples.target: Me duelen mucho los pies y no me apetece salir.
examples.gloss: My feet hurt a lot and I do not feel like going out.

levels.intro: B1 adds the two tenses that share one stem set, the future and the conditional, completes the past with the pluscuamperfecto, and then spends most of its length on one thing: the present subjunctive and every clause that governs it. Note the ceiling. Only the present subjunctive belongs at this level, so the counterfactual si tuviera dinero, viajaría is deliberately not taught here.

topics.title: The future imperfect
topics.summary: One ending set added to the whole infinitive, with twelve irregular stems in three groups: an inserted d, a lost vowel, and a shortened stem. Beyond prediction it carries probability in the present, which is one of its commonest uses. Latin America leans heavily on ir a plus infinitive for real futures and reserves the -ré forms largely for conjecture.
tables:
hablaré hablarás hablará hablaremos hablaréis hablarán

inserted d: tendr- pondr- saldr- vendr- valdr-
lost vowel: podr- sabr- querr- habr-
shortened:  har- dir-

probability: Serán las once. Estará en casa.

examples.target: No contesta, estará reunido. Le llamaré más tarde.
examples.gloss: He is not answering, he must be in a meeting. I will call him later.

topics.title: The conditional simple
topics.summary: The same stems as the future with the endings of the imperfect of -er and -ir verbs. At this level its work is politeness, advice and softened opinion rather than hypothesis, because the hypothetical construction depends on a subjunctive that belongs to the level above.
tables:
hablaría hablarías hablaría hablaríamos hablaríais hablarían

politeness: ¿Podría ayudarme? Querría un billete.
advice:     Deberías descansar. Yo en tu lugar iría.

examples.target: ¿Podría decirme dónde está la salida? Yo que usted preguntaría en información.
examples.gloss: Could you tell me where the exit is? If I were you I would ask at the information desk.

topics.title: The pluscuamperfecto
topics.summary: haber in the imperfect plus the participle, for something already finished before another past moment. It is what lets a narrative step backwards without losing its thread.
tables:
había hablado    habíamos hablado
habías hablado   habíais hablado
había hablado    habían hablado

examples.target: Cuando llegué, ya se habían ido.
examples.gloss: When I arrived, they had already left.

topics.title: Reported speech
topics.summary: Reporting in the present changes only the person and the deixis. Reporting with a past verb shifts the tense back one step: present becomes imperfect, indefinido and perfecto become pluscuamperfecto, future becomes conditional. Questions are reported with si for yes-or-no and with the question word otherwise, and the written accent on the question word stays.
tables:
presente      -> imperfecto
indefinido    -> pluscuamperfecto
p. perfecto   -> pluscuamperfecto
futuro        -> condicional

"Estoy cansado"  -> Dijo que estaba cansado.
"¿Vienes?"       -> Preguntó si venía.
"¿Dónde vives?"  -> Preguntó dónde vivía.

examples.target: Me dijo que había estado allí y que volvería el lunes.
examples.gloss: He told me he had been there and that he would come back on Monday.

topics.title: The present subjunctive: formation
topics.summary: Take the yo form of the present indicative, drop the -o and add the endings of the other conjugation. Every irregularity in the yo form is inherited. The -ir stem-changing verbs additionally change in nosotros and vosotros, where the indicative does not. Six verbs are irregular outright.
tables:
hablo -> hable hables hable hablemos habléis hablen
como  -> coma comas coma comamos comáis coman
salgo -> salga salgas salga salgamos salgáis salgan

-ir extra change: durmamos, pidamos, sintamos
irregular: sea esté vaya dé sepa haya
spelling:  busque llegue empiece coja siga

examples.target: Espero que tengas suerte y que todo salga bien.
examples.gloss: I hope you have luck and that everything goes well.

topics.title: The subjunctive in independent clauses
topics.summary: ojalá always takes it. quizá, tal vez and posiblemente take either, and the choice is meaningful: the subjunctive makes the doubt stronger. a lo mejor and seguramente take the indicative despite meaning much the same thing, which has to be learned rather than reasoned out.
tables:
Ojalá (que) venga.            always subjunctive
Quizá venga. / Quizá viene.   both, subj = more doubt
A lo mejor viene.             always indicative
Que te mejores.               wish with que

examples.target: Ojalá haga buen tiempo, aunque a lo mejor llueve.
examples.gloss: I hope the weather is good, though it may well rain.

topics.title: The subjunctive in noun clauses
topics.summary: A main verb of wanting, asking, advising, forbidding, emotion or value judgement puts the subordinate clause in the subjunctive. So does a verb of doubt or denial, while its affirmative counterpart of certainty takes the indicative. The two clauses must have different subjects; with one subject Spanish uses an infinitive instead.
tables:
querer, pedir, aconsejar, recomendar, prohibir + que + subj
alegrarse de, molestar, sentir, esperar + que + subj
es bueno / importante / necesario + que + subj

no creo que sea      vs   creo que es
dudo que venga       vs   estoy seguro de que viene

same subject -> infinitive:  Quiero ir. NOT *Quiero que yo vaya.

examples.target: Es importante que llegues pronto, pero no creo que haya mucho tráfico.
examples.gloss: It is important that you arrive early, but I do not think there will be much traffic.

topics.title: The negative imperative
topics.summary: Every negative order is the present subjunctive, at all four persons. The pronouns, which attach to the end of an affirmative order, move in front of the verb as soon as no appears. Nothing else about them changes.
tables:
affirmative     negative
tú       dímelo          no me lo digas
vosotros decídselo       no se lo digáis
usted    dígamelo        no me lo diga
ustedes  díganmelo       no me lo digan

examples.target: Cómpralo si quieres, pero no se lo digas a nadie.
examples.gloss: Buy it if you want, but do not tell anyone.

topics.title: Time clauses pointing at the future
topics.summary: cuando, en cuanto, hasta que, mientras, después de que and tan pronto como take the indicative for a fact or a habit and the subjunctive when the moment has not yet arrived. antes de que is the exception that always takes the subjunctive. Spanish never uses a future tense after these conjunctions.
tables:
Cuando llego, como.        habit    -> indicative
Cuando llegué, comí.       past     -> indicative
Cuando llegue, comeré.     future   -> subjunctive

antes de que + subjunctive  (always)
NEVER *cuando llegaré

examples.target: En cuanto termines, avísame, y hazlo antes de que cierren.
examples.gloss: As soon as you finish, let me know, and do it before they close.

topics.title: Purpose, concession and the other adverbial clauses
topics.summary: para que always takes the subjunctive and always has two subjects. aunque takes the indicative for a known fact and the subjunctive to concede something unknown or already granted. Manner and place clauses with como and donde follow the same known-or-unknown split. Consecutive clauses with así que and de modo que take the indicative when they report a result.
tables:
para que + subj:  Te lo doy para que lo uses.
aunque + ind:     Aunque llueve, salgo.   (it is raining)
aunque + subj:    Aunque llueva, saldré.  (it may rain)
como/donde + ind: known    + subj: unknown
así que, de modo que + ind (result)

examples.target: Aunque sea tarde, llámame para que sepa que has llegado.
examples.gloss: Even if it is late, call me so that I know you have arrived.

topics.title: Real conditions
topics.summary: A condition with si that is presented as possible takes the present indicative in the si clause and a present, future or imperative in the other. Spanish never puts a present subjunctive directly after si. The other conditional conjunctions, siempre que, con tal de que, a menos que and en caso de que, do take the subjunctive.
tables:
Si tengo tiempo, voy.
Si llueve, no saldremos.
Si puedes, llámame.

NEVER *si tenga

siempre que / con tal de que / a menos que
en caso de que            + subjunctive

examples.target: Si puedes, ven esta tarde, a menos que tengas otra cosa.
examples.gloss: If you can, come this afternoon, unless you have something else on.

topics.title: Comparative clauses
topics.summary: A2 compares two things (más alto que Juan). B1 compares a thing against a whole clause, which needs a relative structure: más de lo que for quantity or degree, and igual de ... que for equality. Note the trap an A2 learner walks into: with a following clause Spanish uses de lo que and not que, so es más difícil de lo que parece is correct and es más difícil que parece is not.
tables:
compared with a NOUN     más difícil que el otro
compared with a CLAUSE   más difícil de lo que parece
equality with an adj.    igual de difícil que el otro
quantity                 más de lo que esperaba
                         menos de lo que cuesta

examples.target: El examen fue más fácil de lo que esperábamos.
examples.gloss: The exam was easier than we expected.

examples.target: Este piso es igual de céntrico que el anterior.
examples.gloss: This flat is just as central as the previous one.

topics.title: The relative system
topics.summary: que is the general relative for people and things. quien and el que appear after a preposition or with a human antecedent. donde, cuando and como serve as relatives of place, time and manner, cuyo expresses possession and agrees with the thing possessed, and lo que and lo cual refer back to a whole idea rather than a noun. A comma changes a defining clause into an incidental one, and with it the meaning.
tables:
el libro que compré
la persona con quien hablé / con la que hablé
el pueblo donde nací
el autor cuya novela leímos
No entendí lo que dijo.

Los alumnos que aprobaron... (only some did)
Los alumnos, que aprobaron,... (all of them did)

examples.target: La empresa para la que trabajo tiene una sede cuyo edificio es muy antiguo.
examples.gloss: The company I work for has an office whose building is very old.

topics.title: Relative clauses with the subjunctive
topics.summary: When the antecedent is known to exist, the relative clause takes the indicative. When it is being described rather than identified, and may not exist at all, it takes the subjunctive. This is the cleanest illustration in the language of what the subjunctive actually marks.
tables:
Tengo un piso que tiene terraza.   (it exists)
Busco un piso que tenga terraza.   (it may not)

No hay nadie que sepa alemán.
¿Conoces a alguien que pueda ayudarme?

examples.target: Necesito un trabajo que me deje tiempo libre, pero no conozco ninguno que sea así.
examples.gloss: I need a job that leaves me free time, but I do not know of any that is like that.

topics.title: Impersonal and passive se
topics.summary: Impersonal se leaves the agent unnamed and keeps the verb in the third person singular. Passive se promotes the thing affected to subject, so the verb agrees with it and can be plural. The two look identical in the singular and are told apart by whether a plural forces agreement.
tables:
impersonal:  Aquí se come bien.  Se vive tranquilo.
passive:     Se vende piso.  Se venden pisos.
             Se habla español.  Se hablan tres idiomas.

also: dicen que...  la gente dice...  uno nunca sabe

examples.target: En este barrio se vive bien y se alquilan pisos a buen precio.
examples.gloss: You live well in this neighbourhood and flats are rented out at a good price.

topics.title: Verb periphrases
topics.summary: Chains of a verb plus an infinitive, gerund or participle that express aspect: beginning, repeating, stopping, continuing, and how far something has got. They are how Spanish says in one clause what English often needs an adverb for.
tables:
empezar a + inf     start
volver a + inf      do again
acabar de + inf     have just
dejar de + inf      stop
ponerse a + inf     set about
soler + inf         usually

seguir + ger        keep on
llevar + ger        have been -ing for
ir + ger            gradually

llevar + part       have done so far
tener + part        have accumulated

examples.target: Acabo de llegar y ya llevo trabajando dos horas.
examples.gloss: I have just arrived and I have already been working for two hours.

topics.title: ser and estar revisited
topics.summary: Beyond the definition-against-state split, a group of adjectives changes meaning depending on the verb, and estar plus a participle states the result of an action rather than the action itself. This is where the two verbs stop being a beginner's rule and become a choice of meaning.
tables:
es listo   clever      está listo   ready
es bueno   good        está bueno   tasty / well
es rico    wealthy     está rico    delicious
es verde   green       está verde   unripe
es aburrido boring     está aburrido bored

estar + participle: La puerta está cerrada.

examples.target: El informe está listo, y es bueno, aunque el tema es aburrido.
examples.gloss: The report is ready, and it is good, though the topic is boring.

topics.title: por and para in full
topics.summary: para looks forwards to a destination, a purpose, a deadline, a recipient or an opinion holder. por looks backwards to a cause, or sideways to a route, a duration, an exchange or a means. The clearest test case is trabajo para ella against trabajo por ella.
tables:
para: Salgo para Madrid.  Es para ti.  Para el lunes.
      Estudio para aprobar.  Para mí, es fácil.
por:  Lo hago por ti.  Pagué 10 euros por el libro.
      Paso por tu casa.  Por correo.  Por dos meses.

trabajo para ella = she is my employer
trabajo por ella  = I am covering for her

examples.target: Gracias por venir. Este paquete es para tu hermana.
examples.gloss: Thanks for coming. This parcel is for your sister.

topics.title: Verbs and the prepositions they govern
topics.summary: A large group of common verbs takes a fixed preposition that no rule predicts and that rarely matches the English one. They have to be stored as a unit, verb plus preposition, in the way nouns are stored with their article.
tables:
soñar con        acordarse de     fijarse en
contar con       olvidarse de     insistir en
depender de      tratar de        pensar en
enamorarse de    quedar en        confiar en
aprender a       ayudar a         empezar a

examples.target: No me acuerdo de su nombre, pero cuento con que él se acuerde.
examples.gloss: I do not remember his name, but I am counting on him remembering.

topics.title: Verbs of change
topics.summary: Spanish splits to become into several verbs by the kind of change: sudden and emotional, involuntary and lasting, deliberate and achieved, or resulting from a process. Choosing the wrong one is grammatical but immediately non-native.
tables:
ponerse + adj      sudden, temporary   se puso rojo
volverse + adj     lasting, involuntary se volvió desconfiado
hacerse + noun/adj deliberate, gradual  se hizo médico
quedarse + adj     result of an event   se quedó sordo
llegar a ser       reached after effort llegó a ser director
convertirse en     transformation       se convirtió en un éxito

examples.target: Se puso nervioso cuando supo que se había quedado sin trabajo.
examples.gloss: He got nervous when he found out he had been left without a job.

topics.title: Discourse connectors and text organisation
topics.summary: The words that turn a list of sentences into an argument: adding, contrasting, concluding, exemplifying and summarising. B1 writing is graded partly on cohesion, so these are exam content and not decoration.
tables:
adding:      además, también, asimismo
contrasting: sin embargo, en cambio, por el contrario
cause:       ya que, puesto que, debido a, gracias a
result:      por lo tanto, así que, por eso
ordering:    en primer lugar, por un lado / por otro
example:     por ejemplo, es decir
closing:     en resumen, en conclusión, para terminar

examples.target: Por un lado es más barato; sin embargo, está muy lejos, así que no me convence.
examples.gloss: On the one hand it is cheaper; however, it is very far away, so it does not convince me.
